items.followUp: Why should a suspension be shaken before use?

rubric.why: Checks that stirring redistributes the paint pigment.
rubric.description: Stirring distributes the pigment uniformly throughout the paint.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that stirring makes the pigment or colour evenly distributed.

rubric.why: Checks why paint needs to be stirred before use.
rubric.description: Pigment particles may settle on standing, so stirring mixes them back in.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning that particles settle and stirring resuspends or remixes them.

modelAnswer: Paint contains pigment particles that may settle when it stands.
We stir it thoroughly to redistribute the pigment and make the paint uniform before use.

items.followUp: Name two metals that react vigorously with water.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of highly reactive metals.
rubric.description: Names one very reactive metal, such as sodium or potassium.
rubric.how: Award for any one correct example.

rubric.why: The question asks for two examples.
rubric.description: Names a second very reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award for a second correct example; do not award twice for the same metal.

modelAnswer: Sodium is a very reactive metal.
Potassium is another very reactive metal.

items.followUp: State two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Checks a physical property that distinguishes many non-metals.
rubric.description: Gives one correct physical property of non-metals, such as brittleness or poor conductivity.
rubric.how: Award for one correct property; accept appropriate qualifiers such as ‘usually’.

rubric.why: The question asks for two properties.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award for a different correct property; do not award twice for the same property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Solid non-metals are generally brittle and are not malleable or ductile.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of a practical use of platinum.
rubric.description: Gives one valid use of platinum, such as jewellery or as a catalyst.
rubric.how: Award for one valid use.

rubric.why: The question asks for two uses.
rubric.description: Gives a second valid use of platinum.
rubric.how: Award for a different valid use; do not award twice for the same use.

modelAnswer: Platinum is used to make jewellery.
Platinum is used as a catalyst, for example in catalytic converters.

items.followUp: Define an atom and name three kinds of molecules according to the number of atoms in them.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of a molecule.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the smallest particle and 1 mark for independent existence or retaining the substance’s properties.

rubric.why: Checks identification of one molecular type by atom count.
rubric.description: Names the monoatomic type of molecule.
rubric.how: Award for naming monoatomic or describing a molecule with one atom.

rubric.why: Checks identification of another molecular type by atom count.
rubric.description: Names the diatomic type of molecule.
rubric.how: Award for naming diatomic or describing a molecule with two atoms.

rubric.why: Checks identification of a third molecular type.
rubric.description: Names a third type, such as triatomic or polyatomic.
rubric.how: Award for a correct third type distinct from the types already credited.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retains the properties of that substance.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom, for example He.
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms, for example H₂.
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms, for example H₂O.

items.followUp: State four physical properties of covalent compounds.

rubric.why: Checks a characteristic physical property of ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds are crystalline solids.
rubric.how: Award for identifying their crystalline solid nature.

rubric.why: Checks the strong electrostatic attraction in ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds have high melting and/or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for high melting points or high boiling points.

rubric.why: Checks the common solubility property of ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that many ionic compounds are soluble in water.
rubric.how: Award for water solubility, preferably qualified as ‘many’ or ‘usually’.

rubric.why: Checks electrical conductivity when ions can move.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not when solid.
rubric.how: Award for conductivity in the molten or aqueous state; accept an explicit contrast with the solid state.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are crystalline solids.
They generally have high melting and boiling points.
Many ionic compounds are soluble in water.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Write three differences between the atomic models of Thomson and Rutherford.

rubric.why: Checks Rutherford’s view of where positive charge is located compared with Bohr’s model.
rubric.description: Contrasts Rutherford’s concentrated positive nucleus with Bohr’s positive nucleus and electron shells.
rubric.how: Award when the answer identifies the positive charge as concentrated in a small nucleus in Rutherford’s model, rather than spread through the atom.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr’s key addition to the nuclear model.
rubric.description: States that Bohr proposed fixed, permitted orbits or energy levels for electrons.
rubric.how: Award for fixed shells, orbits, or quantized energy levels.

rubric.why: Checks the contrast with Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model did not specify fixed electron energy levels or permitted orbits.
rubric.how: Award for describing Rutherford’s electrons as not restricted to Bohr-like fixed energy levels.

rubric.why: Checks the classical difficulty with Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Explains that in Rutherford’s model orbiting electrons would radiate energy and lose it continuously.
rubric.how: Award for the predicted energy loss or radiation by orbiting electrons.

rubric.why: Checks what Bohr’s postulates explained or changed.
rubric.description: States that Bohr’s stationary orbits have no energy loss and help explain atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast such as stationary orbits, atomic stability, or explaining the hydrogen line spectrum.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model has a small, positively charged nucleus; Bohr’s model also has a nucleus but adds electron shells around it.
In Rutherford’s model, electrons were not assigned fixed energy levels; in Bohr’s model, electrons occupy only permitted orbits with definite energies.
Rutherford’s model allowed electrons to orbit at different distances; Bohr’s model restricts them to fixed energy levels.
According to classical theory, Rutherford’s orbiting electrons would radiate energy and lose it continuously; Bohr’s electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability or the hydrogen line spectrum; Bohr’s model explained both.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the pressure of vapour and its equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of change.

rubric.why: Checks how the liquid’s nature affects vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that more volatile liquids or liquids with weaker intermolecular attractions have higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for a correct relationship between volatility or intermolecular forces and vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Clarifies a commonly confused factor while addressing factors affecting vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Notes that surface area affects how quickly equilibrium is reached, but not the equilibrium vapour pressure at a given temperature.
rubric.how: Award for this distinction; do not accept a claim that surface area changes the equilibrium vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour when it is in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
Increasing the temperature increases the vapour pressure.
A more volatile liquid, with weaker intermolecular forces, has a higher vapour pressure.
Surface area affects how quickly equilibrium is reached, but does not change the equilibrium vapour pressure at a fixed temperature.
